title: Learning from the Unseen: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Hidden Actions

paper.title: Learning from the Unseen: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Hidden Actions
paper.abstract: Abstract Standard offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically assume that the actions in the dataset are observed without error. However, in many real-world applications, the true actions are unobserved and only noisy proxies are available, causing existing RL methods to yield biased and potentially misleading conclusions. We study off-policy evaluation in infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes with hidden actions. By leveraging the next-state variable as a natural proxy for the unobserved action, we establish identification of the policy value and propose an influence-function-based estimator: LURE ( L earning from the U nseen: R obust E stimator). LURE is multiply robust—remaining consistent under several combinations of correctly specified nuisance components—and is asymptotically normal, enabling valid statistical inference. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address offline RL with hidden actions. We demonstrate LURE’s effectiveness via simulations and a sepsis management application using the MIMIC-III database.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 , RL;) aims to maximize the long-run cumulative reward in sequential decision-making by learning a policy that maps states to distributions over actions. In recent years, RL has been successfully applied to a wide range of domains, including game playing ( Silver et al., 2016 ) , robotics ( Levine et al., 2020 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) , business strategy ( Den Boer, 2015 ; Bian et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , healthcare ( Liao et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , and social science ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Recent advances in large language models have also drawn heavily on RL techniques; see, for example, Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Rafailov et al. (2023) . RL is also closely connected to the statistical literature on dynamic treatment regimes and precision medicine ( Murphy, 2003 ; Robins, 2004 ; Qian and Murphy, 2011 ; Zhao et al., 2012 ; Zhang et al., 2012 ; Wallace and Moodie, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Kitagawa and Tetenov, 2018 ; Shi et al., 2018 ; Qi et al., 2020 ; Athey and Wager, 2021 ; Cui and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2021 ; Bian et al., 2023 ; Shen and Cui, 2024 ) . This line of work studies how to tailor treatment decisions to individual patients so as to optimize expected clinical outcomes, typically over a finite number of treatment stages. While the goals are closely aligned with those of RL, most existing statistical methods for precision medicine are not designed for large- or infinite-horizon problems. In this paper, we focus on off-policy evaluation (OPE), a fundamental problem in offline reinforcement learning. The goal of OPE is to estimate the long-run value of a target policy using historical data generated under a potentially different behavior policy. Existing model-free OPE methods broadly fall into three classes: direct methods ( Ernst et al., 2005 ; Le et al., 2019 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Chen and Qi, 2022 ) , importance-sampling-based methods ( Precup, 2000 ; Liu et al., 2018 ; Nachum et al., 2019 ; Uehara et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and doubly robust methods ( Jiang and Li, 2016 ; Thomas and Brunskill, 2016 ; Kallus and Uehara, 2022 ; Liao et al., 2022 ) . See Uehara et al. (2022) for a comprehensive overview. Most of the existing literature assumes that the action recorded in the offline dataset is observed without error. In many applications, however, the action of scientific or operational interest may be partially observed or entirely latent ( Young et al., 2018 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ) . Such discrepancies can arise from annotation errors, imperfect management systems, indirect action reconstruction from high-dimensional records, privacy-preserving data collection that releases only a coarsened proxy, or an improperly discretized action space. If these discrepancies are ignored, standard OPE methods can target the wrong state–action mechanism and yield misleading policy evaluations. Our work is motivated by the longitudinal sepsis data from the MIMIC-III ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) . This large electronic health record database combines multiple heterogeneous sources and is characterized by irregular measurements, substantial missingness, and complex preprocessing pipelines ( Gupta et al., 2022 ) . As in many EHR-based studies, these features increase the risk of measurement error in downstream analyses ( Rogers et al., 2021 ) . In particular, treatment records may not perfectly reflect the treatment actually delivered because of delayed charting, documentation mistakes, or administrative coding practices. This gap between recorded and true actions makes standard offline RL methods unreliable and motivates principled methods that explicitly account for hidden actions. The hidden-action problem is related to the measurement-error literature. When the action is continuous and observed with additive noise, one can often leverage classical measurement error methods; see, e.g., Carroll et al. (2006) . In contrast, discrete action misclassification is substantially more challenging because the classical additive error framework underlying these methods generally does not apply. A recent related contribution is Zhou and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2024) , which studies causal effect estimation under a hidden treatment in the static setting. Their framework uses a surrogate variable, together with an additional proxy variable related to the hidden treatment, and develops multiply robust estimators using semiparametric efficiency theory. Our work also leverages a proxy for the hidden action to identify the value function and construct an estimator. A key feature of the RL setting is that the next state provides such a proxy naturally: because it depends on the current latent action through the transition dynamics, it contains information about the hidden action that can be exploited for identification. Despite this connection, our setting differs substantially from that of Zhou and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2024) . First, hidden actions arise in a sequential decision-making setting. Consequently, the target parameter and nuisance functions depend on the transition dynamics and the target policy, making the problem substantially more complex than in the static setting. Second, unlike the static hidden-treatment setting, which requires an additional proxy variable, the next state in RL serves simultaneously as a proxy for the current hidden action and as part of the future trajectory. This dual role creates technical challenges that are absent in the single-stage setting. As a result, the identification strategy, influence-function derivation, and asymptotic analysis require new arguments that explicitly exploit the sequential nature of RL, rather than constituting a direct extension of the single-stage hidden-treatment framework. Challenges and contributions . Since the true action in the environment is never observed, off-policy evaluation with hidden actions presents three main challenges. First, the state–action distribution underlying standard OPE methods is latent, making it unclear whether the target policy value is identifiable from the observed data. Second, even when identification can be established, constructing valid estimators remains nontrivial, as naively substituting the latent action with its surrogate in existing OPE methods generally leads to biased estimates. Finally, valid uncertainty quantification and policy comparison procedures have yet to be developed in this setting. To address these challenges, we first establish identification of the target policy value in the presence of hidden actions by leveraging the next-state variable within the RL framework. Second, we derive an observed-data influence function representation and use it to construct LURE ( L earning from the U nseen: R obust E stimator), a multiply robust estimator that remains consistent under several combinations of correctly specified nuisance components. To address the unobserved latent-action problem in the estimation procedure, we propose a novel expectation–maximization-based algorithm for estimating the nuisance functions in our offline RL setting. Finally, we establish finite-sample error bounds and the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator, enabling valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for policy value estimation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to study offline reinforcement learning in the hidden-action setting. Organization . The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we review the standard RL framework and existing OPE methods. In Sections 3 and 4 , we introduce the hidden-action setting, establish identification, and construct the LURE estimator. In Section 5 , we present the large-sample theory for LURE. In Section 6 , we report simulation results, and in Section 7 we present the MIMIC-III sepsis analysis. We conclude with a discussion in Section 8 . All proofs are deferred to the Appendix.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: In this section, we briefly review the standard RL framework, in which actions are perfectly recorded. We consider a time-homogeneous Markov decision process (MDP) defined by the sequence { ( S t , A t , R t ) } t ≥ 1 \{(S_{t},A_{t},R_{t})\}_{t\geq 1} , where S t ∈ 𝒮 S_{t}\in\mathcal{S} denotes the state, A t ∈ 𝒜 A_{t}\in\mathcal{A} the action, and R t ∈ ℝ R_{t}\in\mathbb{R} the reward at time t t . The system dynamics are governed by a stationary Markov transition kernel q ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) q(\cdot\mid s,a) . Specifically, given the current state-action pair ( S t , A t ) = ( s , a ) (S_{t},A_{t})=(s,a) , the next state is sampled according to S t + 1 ∼ q ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) S_{t+1}\sim q(\cdot\mid s,a) , independent of the preceding history. The reward R t R_{t} is generated from a time-invariant distribution conditioned on ( S t , A t ) (S_{t},A_{t}) for any time t t . We define the reward function θ R ​ ( s , a ) \theta_{R}(s,a) as the conditional expectation: θ R ( s , a ) := 𝔼 [ R t ∣ S t = s , A t = a ] . \displaystyle\theta_{R}(s,a):=\mathbb{E}[R_{t}\mid S_{t}=s,A_{t}=a]. As is standard in the reinforcement learning literature, throughout, we assume the environment is stationary, meaning that both the transition kernel q q and the reward function θ R \theta_{R} are Markovian and remain constant over time. This assumption lays the foundation for many state-of-the-art algorithms ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) . Under this setting, it is sufficient to focus on stationary policies π \pi under which A t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ S t ) A_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid S_{t}) ( Puterman, 2014 ) . Such a stationary policy specifies how the agent selects actions at each decision time, mapping the current state to a distribution over actions. Figure 1 summarizes the data-generating process in the standard MDP setting described above. Policy evaluation aims to estimate the expected reward under a target policy π \pi . This is quantified by the value function, which measures the long-term performance of a policy and is defined as: V ⁡ ( π ) := 𝔼 S 1 ∼ p e ​ [ 𝔼 π ​ ( ∑ t = 1 ∞ γ t − 1 ​ R t | S 1 ) ] , \displaystyle V(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{S_{1}\sim p_{e}}\left[\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\gamma^{t-1}R_{t}\,\middle|\,S_{1}\right)\right], (1) where γ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor that governs the trade-off between immediate and future rewards, and p e p_{e} is a known initial state distribution. Finally, we introduce a doubly robust representation ( Kallus and Uehara, 2022 ) of the value function, which combines the ideas of the previous two methods. Specifically, we have V ⁡ ( π ) = 𝔼 p e ​ ( V π ​ ( S ) ) + ( 1 − γ ) − 1 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ω ⁡ ( S , A ) ​ [ R + γ ​ V π ​ ( S ′ ) − Q π ​ ( S , A ) ] ] . \displaystyle V(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{e}}(V^{\pi}(S))+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\omega(S,A)\left[R+\gamma V^{\pi}(S^{\prime})-Q^{\pi}(S,A)\right]\Big]. The key advantage of this doubly robust formulation is that the resulting estimator remains consistent if either the Q Q -function or the density ratio is correctly specified. The aforementioned OPE identification results and estimation methods all rely on the assumption that actions are perfectly measured in the offline data. In many applications, however, the decision-maker only has access to an error-prone observed action A ~ t ∈ 𝒜 \widetilde{A}_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , which is a noisy measurement of the underlying true action A t A_{t} . We address this setting in the following section.

This motivates us to employ a weighted version of fitted Q Q -evaluation ( Ernst et al., 2005 , FQE,) . We summarize the estimation procedure in Algorithm 1 . We therefore adopt an iterative scheme that alternates between updating the generative components given the current posterior (the M-step) and recomputing the posterior given the updated components (the E-step). In the M-step, the behavior policy, measurement model, and conditional means of the reward and next state are updated via weighted least-squares regressions with weights η ^ ( k ) \widehat{\eta}^{(k)} , while the conditional densities q q and h h are updated via weighted maximum likelihood. Finally, we introduce the LURE estimator with a K K -fold cross-fitting procedure ( Schick, 1986 ; Chernozhukov et al., 2018 ) , which mitigates overfitting bias and helps control the empirical-process remainder. Specifically, partition the N N trajectories into K K folds { I k } k = 1 K \{I_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} of approximately equal size. sections.heading: 5 Theory
sections.text: In this section, we establish the theoretical properties of the cross-fitted LURE estimator V ^ ​ ( π ) \widehat{V}(\pi) , showing that it achieves N ​ T \sqrt{NT} -consistency and asymptotic normality. These results enable the construction of asymptotically valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the policy value V ⁡ ( π ) V(\pi) . For later use, we introduce some notation. Let ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denote the L 2 ​ ( P ) L_{2}(P) norm under the data-generating distribution, and let ∥ ⋅ ∥ ∞ \|\cdot\|_{\infty} denote the supremum norm. For each action-indexed estimated nuisance function f ^ ∈ { ω ^ , θ ^ A ~ , θ ^ R , θ ^ S ′ } \widehat{f}\in\{\widehat{\omega},\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}},\widehat{\theta}_{R},\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}\} , define δ ​ f ^ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) = f ^ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − f ⁡ ( ⋅ , a ) \delta\widehat{f}(\cdot,a)=\widehat{f}(\cdot,a)-f(\cdot,a) , a ∈ { 0 , 1 } a\in\{0,1\} . Define e M ( S , a ) = 𝔼 [ V ^ π ( S ′ ) ∣ S , A = a ] − ℳ ​ V π ^ ( S , a ) . e_{M}(S,a)=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{V}^{\pi}(S^{\prime})\mid S,A=a]-\widehat{\mathcal{M}V^{\pi}}(S,a). We begin with the following technical conditions. Assumption 5.1 (Regularity conditions) . (i) (Boundedness) All the nuisance estimators are uniformly bounded. (ii) (Separation) There exists some universal constant c > 0 c>0 such that, for all a a , inf s | θ A ~ ​ ( s , a ) − θ A ~ ​ ( s , 1 − a ) | ≥ c , \inf_{s}\left|\theta_{\widetilde{A}}(s,a)-\theta_{\widetilde{A}}(s,1-a)\right|\geq c, inf s | θ R ​ ( s , a ) − θ R ​ ( s , 1 − a ) | ≥ c \inf_{s}\left|\theta_{R}(s,a)-\theta_{R}(s,1-a)\right|\geq c and inf s | θ S ′ ​ ( s , a ) − θ S ′ ​ ( s , 1 − a ) | ≥ c . \inf_{s}\left|\theta_{S^{\prime}}(s,a)-\theta_{S^{\prime}}(s,1-a)\right|\geq c. The same lower bounds hold almost surely when θ A ~ \theta_{\widetilde{A}} , θ R \theta_{R} , and θ S ′ \theta_{S^{\prime}} are replaced by their estimated counterparts. Assumption 5.1 (i) is a standard boundedness condition. Assumption 5.1 (ii) is a separation condition; such conditions are common in causal inference and policy learning, see, e.g., Qian and Murphy (2011) ; Zhou and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2024) . It ensures that the denominators appearing in the influence function are bounded away from zero. Intuitively, it requires the hidden actions to induce meaningfully different conditional laws for the surrogate action, reward, and next-state proxy. Theorem 3 (Error Bound) . Under Assumptions 3.1 and 5.1 , we have V ^ ( π ) − V ( π ) = 1 N ​ T ∑ i = 1 N ∑ t = 1 T φ π ( O i , t ) + O p ( L n + I n ) + o p ( ( N T ) − 1 / 2 ) , \widehat{V}(\pi)-V(\pi)=\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varphi^{\pi}(O_{i,t})+O_{p}(L_{n}+I_{n})+o_{p}((NT)^{-1/2}), where L n = max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ⁡ ‖ δ ​ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ κ , L_{n}=\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|^{\kappa}, for some κ > 0 , \kappa>0, is the label-selection error, and I n = ∑ a ∈ { 0 , 1 } 𝔼 [ { | δ θ ^ A ~ ( S , a ) | + | δ θ ^ S ′ ( S , a ) | + | δ ω ^ ( S , a ) | } | δ θ ^ R ( S , a ) | \displaystyle I_{n}=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\mathbb{E}\Big[\left\{|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,a)|+|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(S,a)|+|\delta\widehat{\omega}(S,a)|\right\}|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{R}(S,a)| + { | δ ​ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( S , a ) | + | δ ​ θ ^ R ​ ( S , a ) | + | δ ​ ω ^ ​ ( S , a ) | } ​ | e M ​ ( S , a ) | \displaystyle+\left\{|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,a)|+|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{R}(S,a)|+|\delta\widehat{\omega}(S,a)|\right\}|e_{M}(S,a)| + | δ ​ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( S , a ) | ​ | δ ​ θ ^ S ′ ​ ( S , a ) | + | δ ​ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( S , 1 − a ) ​ ‖ δ ​ θ ^ S ′ ​ ( S , 1 − a ) ‖ ​ δ ​ θ ^ R ​ ( S , a ) | \displaystyle+|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(S,a)|+|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,1-a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(S,1-a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{R}(S,a)| + | δ ω ^ ( S , a ) | | δ θ ^ A ~ ( S , 1 − a ) | | δ θ ^ S ′ ( S , 1 − a ) | + | δ ω ^ ( S , a ) | | δ θ ^ A ~ ( S , 1 − a ) | | δ θ ^ R ( S , 1 − a ) | ] \displaystyle+|\delta\widehat{\omega}(S,a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,1-a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(S,1-a)|+|\delta\widehat{\omega}(S,a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(S,1-a)||\delta\widehat{\theta}_{R}(S,1-a)|\Big] is the second order remainder. Theorem 3 decomposes the policy evaluation error into the sample average of the influence function, together with a label-selection remainder L n L_{n} , a second-order remainder I n I_{n} , and a negligible remainder of order o p ( ( N T ) − 1 / 2 ) o_{p}((NT)^{-1/2}) . We make several remarks. First, the exponent κ > 0 \kappa>0 governs the decay rate of the label-selection remainder L n L_{n} ; its exact value depends on the regularity of the label selector and only affects the rate at which L n L_{n} converges to zero. Second, under suitable convergence rate conditions on the nuisance function estimators, both L n L_{n} and I n I_{n} are o p ( ( N T ) − 1 / 2 ) o_{p}((NT)^{-1/2}) , so that the influence-function term dominates the asymptotic expansion. Finally, the remainder I n I_{n} consists of products of nuisance estimation errors, which gives rise to a multiple robustness property for consistency, as formalized below. Corollary 1 (Multiple Robustness) . Suppose that the assumptions in Theorem 3 hold and the label-alignment step is consistent. Then we have V ^ ​ ( π ) − V ⁡ ( π ) = o p ​ ( 1 ) , \displaystyle\widehat{V}(\pi)-V(\pi)=o_{p}(1), provided that for each a ∈ { 0 , 1 } a\in\{0,1\} , at least one of the following conditions is satisfied: (i) ‖ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , ‖ θ ^ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{R}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{R}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , and ‖ e M ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|e_{M}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) ; (ii) ‖ θ ^ S ′ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ S ′ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{S^{\prime}}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , ‖ θ ^ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{R}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{R}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , and ‖ e M ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|e_{M}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) ; (iii) ‖ ω ^ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − ω ⁡ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\omega}(\cdot,a)-\omega(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , ‖ θ ^ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ R ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{R}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{R}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , and ‖ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) ; (iv) ‖ ω ^ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − ω ⁡ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\omega}(\cdot,a)-\omega(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , ‖ θ ^ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ A ~ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , ‖ θ ^ S ′ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) − θ S ′ ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(\cdot,a)-\theta_{S^{\prime}}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) , and ‖ e M ​ ( ⋅ , a ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) \|e_{M}(\cdot,a)\|=o_{p}(1) . The four cases in Corollary 1 highlight two complementary routes to consistency. Cases (i) and (ii) correspond to a direct-estimation strategy: consistency is achieved when the reward bridge θ R \theta_{R} is estimated consistently together with either the latent-action regression θ A ~ \theta_{\widetilde{A}} or the next-state regression θ S ′ \theta_{S^{\prime}} , provided that the continuation-value error e M e_{M} is negligible. In contrast, Cases (iii) and (iv) correspond to an MIS-based strategy: once ω \omega and θ A ~ \theta_{\widetilde{A}} are consistently estimated, consistency is preserved as long as either θ R \theta_{R} or θ S ′ \theta_{S^{\prime}} is correctly specified. This multiple robustness property allows misspecification in one component of the debiasing structure to be offset by correct specification of another. Asymptotic normality . We next strengthen the consistency result to an asymptotic normality result. Let α ω , α A ~ , α R , α S ′ , α M , α min ≥ 0 \alpha_{\omega},\alpha_{\widetilde{A}},\alpha_{R},\alpha_{S^{\prime}},\alpha_{M},\alpha_{\min}\geq 0 such that max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ δ ω ^ ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ = O p ( ( N T ) − α ω ) , max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ δ θ ^ A ~ ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ = O p ( ( N T ) − α A ~ ) , max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ δ θ ^ R ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ = O p ( ( N T ) − α R ) , max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ δ θ ^ S ′ ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ = O p ( ( N T ) − α S ′ ) , max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ e M ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ = O p ( ( N T ) − α M ) , α min = min ( α ω , α A ~ , α R , α S ′ , α M ) . \begin{gathered}\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\omega}(\cdot,a)\|=O_{p}((NT)^{-\alpha_{\omega}}),\qquad\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|=O_{p}((NT)^{-\alpha_{\widetilde{A}}}),\\ \max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{R}(\cdot,a)\|=O_{p}((NT)^{-\alpha_{R}}),\qquad\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{S^{\prime}}(\cdot,a)\|=O_{p}((NT)^{-\alpha_{S^{\prime}}}),\\ \max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|e_{M}(\cdot,a)\|=O_{p}((NT)^{-\alpha_{M}}),\qquad\alpha_{\min}=\min\left(\alpha_{\omega},\alpha_{\widetilde{A}},\alpha_{R},\alpha_{S^{\prime}},\alpha_{M}\right).\end{gathered} Under additional rate conditions α min > 1 / 4 \alpha_{\min}>1/4 , the LURE estimator admits the expansion V ^ ( π ) − V ( π ) = 1 N ​ T ∑ i = 1 N ∑ t = 1 T φ π ( O i , t ) + o p ( ( N T ) − 1 / 2 ) . \displaystyle\widehat{V}(\pi)-V(\pi)=\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varphi^{\pi}(O_{i,t})+o_{p}((NT)^{-1/2}). Consequently, asymptotic normality follows by applying the martingale central limit theorem ( McLeish, 1974 ) to the leading term. Theorem 4 (Asymptotic normality) . Under Assumptions 3.1 and 5.1 , suppose further that α min > 1 / 4 \alpha_{\min}>1/4 and, for some κ > 0 \kappa>0 , max a ∈ { 0 , 1 } ∥ δ θ ^ A ~ ( ⋅ , a ) ∥ κ = o p ( ( N T ) − 1 / 2 ) . \max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\|\delta\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{A}}(\cdot,a)\|^{\kappa}=o_{p}((NT)^{-1/2}). We have N ​ T ​ ( V ^ ​ ( π ) − V ⁡ ( π ) ) → 𝑑 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ π 2 ) , \sqrt{NT}\big(\widehat{V}(\pi)-V(\pi)\big)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}\big(0,\sigma^{2}_{\pi}\big), where σ π 2 = Var ​ ( φ π ​ ( O ) ) \sigma^{2}_{\pi}={\mbox{Var}}(\varphi^{\pi}(O)) is the variance of the influence function in Equation ( 2 ). Theorem 4 establishes that the proposed estimator is asymptotically normal under the stated rate conditions. sections.heading: 6 Numerical Studies
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed LURE estimator through synthetic experiments and a benchmark dataset. Competing methods . We compare our proposal with representative direct, importance-sampling, and doubly robust estimators that ignore the latent-action structure and instead treat the observed surrogate A ~ \widetilde{A} as if it were the true action. Specifically, we consider the following competing methods: sequential importance sampling ( Precup, 2000 , SIS,) , fitted Q Q evaluation ( Ernst et al., 2005 , FQE,) , least-squares temporal difference ( Shi et al., 2022 , LSTD,) , marginalized importance sampling ( Uehara et al., 2020 , MIS,) , and double reinforcement learning ( Kallus and Uehara, 2022 , DRL,) . Crucially, all five baselines use the observed surrogate A ~ \widetilde{A} in place of the true action, so they are expected to exhibit systematic bias when misclassification is present. Throughout, we set the discount factor to γ = 0.7 \gamma=0.7 , generate N = 50 N=50 independent offline trajectories of length T = 50 T=50 in each replication, and vary the misclassification rate over four scenarios Pr ⁡ ( A ≠ A ~ ) ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } \Pr(A\neq\widetilde{A})\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3\} . The surrogate action is subject to misclassification, generated according to Pr ⁡ ( A ~ ≠ A ) = τ \Pr(\widetilde{A}\neq A)=\tau , independently of ( S , A ) (S,A) ; equivalently, θ A ~ ​ ( s , 1 ) = 1 − τ \theta_{\widetilde{A}}(s,1)=1-\tau and θ A ~ ​ ( s , 0 ) = τ \theta_{\widetilde{A}}(s,0)=\tau for all s s . We consider τ ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } \tau\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3\} , corresponding to Scenarios 1–4. Proxy variable selection . Recall that θ S ′ ( s , a ) = 𝔼 [ l ( S ′ ) ∣ S = s , A = a ] \theta_{S^{\prime}}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[l(S^{\prime})\mid S=s,A=a\right] denotes the conditional expectation of a known feature mapping l ⁡ ( ⋅ ) l(\cdot) of the next state, given the current state and action. In implementation, we restrict attention to coordinate-wise features l ⁡ ( s ) = s ( j ) l(s)=s^{(j)} , the j j -th component of the state variable, so that θ S ′ ( s , a ) = 𝔼 [ S ′ ( j ) ∣ S = s , A = a ] \theta_{S^{\prime}}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[S^{\prime(j)}\mid S=s,A=a\right] represents the corresponding conditional mean. To construct g a ′ ​ ( O ) g_{a}^{\prime}(O) , we select the coordinate j j based on the Pearson partial correlation between S ′ ( j ) S^{\prime(j)} and observed A ~ \widetilde{A} conditional on S S , and choose the coordinate with the largest absolute value.

sections.heading: 7 Real Data Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we apply the proposed method to a sepsis dataset from MIMIC-III ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) , a database containing information on critical care patients from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. We focus on ICU stays with complete observations over 20 decision stages, yielding T = 20 T=20 and N = 500 N=500 . The outcome is the sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score ( Jones et al., 2009 ) , where a larger score indicates more severe organ dysfunction and a higher risk of mortality. Following Bian et al. (2025) , we study a binary intravenous-fluid intervention to illustrate the method in a clinically interpretable setting. Specifically, at each decision time t t , we consider A t ∈ { 0 , 1 } A_{t}\in\{0,1\} , where A t = 1 A_{t}=1 indicates that intravenous fluid is administered and A t = 0 A_{t}=0 indicates no intravenous fluid. The state vector includes 46 demographic, physiological, laboratory, and clinical variables, such as age, gender, weight, and vital signs. We evaluate three target policies. The first policy always administers IV, π iv ​ ( 1 ∣ s ) = 1 . \pi_{\mathrm{iv}}(1\mid s)=1. The second policy never administers IV, namely π noiv ​ ( 1 ∣ s ) = 0 . \pi_{\mathrm{noiv}}(1\mid s)=0. Similarly to Bian et al. (2025) , we also evaluate a SOFA-tailored policy that administers IV when the current SOFA score is at least 3 and no IV otherwise, π ta ​ ( 1 ∣ s ) = 𝟙 ​ ( SOFA ≥ 3 ) . \pi_{\mathrm{ta}}(1\mid s)=\mathds{1}\left(\mathrm{SOFA}\geq 3\right). This policy is motivated by the finding that a SOFA score greater than 2 reflects an overall mortality risk of approximately 10% in a general hospital population with suspected infection ( Singer et al., 2016 ) . We apply the proposed LURE estimator with discount factor γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 . The nuisance functions are estimated using linear features of the state variables. For comparison, we also report the DRL estimator based on FQE and MIS. As in the simulation studies, we construct θ S ′ ​ ( s , a ) \theta_{S^{\prime}}(s,a) using the Pearson partial correlation between each next-state component S ′ ( j ) S^{\prime(j)} and the observed treatment A ~ \widetilde{A} conditional on S S , and choose as the proxy variable the component with the largest absolute partial correlation. Table 2 : Estimated policy values for the MIMIC-III sepsis analysis using DRL and LURE. Smaller values indicate lower expected SOFA scores. Policy DRL estimate DRL 95% CI LURE estimate LURE 95% CI Always IV 66.29 [63.78, 68.79] 62.10 [60.16, 64.04] No IV 67.15 [62.42, 71.88] 68.63 [67.03, 70.22] SOFA-tailored rule 66.91 [64.27, 69.55] 65.92 [64.30, 67.53] Table 2 reports the estimated policy values. Because smaller values correspond to better outcomes, the LURE estimator favors the always-IV policy, with an estimated SOFA score of 62.10, followed by the SOFA-tailored rule at 65.92 and the no-IV policy at 68.63. The 95% confidence interval for the always-IV policy, [60.16, 64.04], does not overlap with the intervals for either the SOFA-tailored rule or the no-IV policy. By contrast, the DRL confidence intervals overlap substantially across all three policies. These results suggest that accounting for the hidden-action structure may lead to different policy evaluations in this sepsis application, highlighting the potential impact of hidden actions on empirical conclusions.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: This paper studies off-policy evaluation when the true action is hidden and only a noisy surrogate is observed. By exploiting the next state as an internal proxy for the hidden action, we establish identification of the policy value and derive an observed-data influence function. The resulting LURE estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, which supports valid large-sample inference under flexible nuisance estimation. A novel EM-based procedure is proposed for estimating the nuisance functions. Across tabular, continuous-state, and OpenAI Gym environments, the simulations show that explicitly accounting for hidden actions can reduce bias relative to standard OPE methods that treat the surrogate action as the truth.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.25241v1 [stat.ML] 28 Jul 2026 Learning from the Unseen: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Hidden Actions Zeyu Bian Ying Zhou Yifan Cui Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Florida State University Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of Connecticut Affiliation: Center for Data Science, Zhejiang University † Equal contribution. * Corresponding authors: yzhou@uconn.edu; cuiyf@zju.edu.cn. Abstract Standard offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically assume that the actions in the dataset are observed without error. However, in many real-world applications, the true actions are unobserved and only noisy proxies are available, causing existing RL methods to yield biased and potentially misleading conclusions. We study off-policy evaluation in infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes with hidden actions. By leveraging the next-state variable as a natural proxy for the unobserved action, we establish identification of the policy value and propose an influence-function-based estimator: LURE ( L earning from the U nseen: R obust E stimator). LURE is multiply robust—remaining consistent under several combinations of correctly specified nuisance components—and is asymptotically normal, enabling valid statistical inference. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address offline RL with hidden actions. We demonstrate LURE’s effectiveness via simulations and a sepsis management application using the MIMIC-III database. Keywords: Reinforcement learning; Off-policy evaluation; Latent action; Multiple robustness 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 , RL;) aims to maximize the long-run cumulative reward in sequential decision-making by learning a policy that maps states to distributions over actions. In recent years, RL has been successfully applied to a wide range of domains, including game playing ( Silver et al., 2016 ) , robotics ( Levine et al., 2020 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) , business strategy ( Den Boer, 2015 ; Bian et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , healthcare ( Liao et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , and social science ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Recent advances in large language models have also drawn heavily on RL techniques; see, for example, Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Rafailov et al. (2023) . RL is also closely connected to the statistical literature on dynamic treatment regimes and precision medicine ( Murphy, 2003 ; Robins, 2004 ; Qian and Murphy, 2011 ; Zhao et al., 2012 ; Zhang et al., 2012 ; Wallace and Moodie, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Kitagawa and Tetenov, 2018 ; Shi et al., 2018 ; Qi et al., 2020 ; Athey and Wager, 2021 ; Cui and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2021 ; Bian et al., 2023 ; Shen and Cui, 2024 ) . This line of work studies how to tailor treatment decisions to individual patients so as to optimize expected clinical outcomes, typically over a finite number of treatment stages. While the goals are closely aligned with those of RL, most existing statistical methods for precision medicine are not designed for large- or infinite-horizon problems. In this paper, we focus on off-policy evaluation (OPE), a fundamental problem in offline reinforcement learning. The goal of OPE is to estimate the long-run value of a target policy using historical data generated under a potentially different behavior policy. Existing model-free OPE methods broadly fall into three classes: direct methods ( Ernst et al., 2005 ; Le et al., 2019 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Chen and Qi, 2022 ) , importance-sampling-based methods ( Precup, 2000 ; Liu et al., 2018 ; Nachum et al., 2019 ; Uehara et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and doubly robust methods ( Jiang and Li, 2016 ; Thomas and Brunskill, 2016 ; Kallus and Uehara, 2022 ; Liao et al., 2022 ) . See Uehara et al. (2022) for a comprehensive overview. Most of the existing literature assumes that the action recorded in the offline dataset is observed without error. In many applications, however, the action of scientific or operational interest may be partially observed or entirely latent ( Young et al., 2018 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ) . Such discrepancies can arise from annotation errors, imperfect management systems, indirect action reconstruction from high-dimensional records, privacy-preserving data collection that releases only a coarsened proxy, or an improperly discretized action space. If these discrepancies are ignored, standard OPE methods can target the wrong state–action mechanism and yield misleading policy evaluations. Our work is motivated by the longitudinal sepsis data from the MIMIC-III ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) . This large electronic health record database combines multiple heterogeneous sources and is characterized by irregular measurements, substantial missingness, and complex preprocessing pipelines ( Gupta et al., 2022 ) . As in many EHR-based studies, these features increase the risk of measurement error in downstream analyses ( Rogers et al., 2021 ) . In particular, treatment records may not perfectly reflect the treatment actually delivered because of delayed charting, documentation mistakes, or administrative coding practices. This gap between recorded and true actions makes standard offline RL methods unreliable and motivates principled methods that explicitly account for hidden actions. The hidden-action problem is related to the measurement-error literature. When the action is continuous and observed with additive noise, one can often leverage classical measurement error methods; see, e.g., Carroll et al. (2006) . In contrast, discrete action misclassification is substantially more challenging because the classical additive error framework underlying these methods generally does not apply. A recent related contribution is Zhou and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2024) , which studies causal effect estimation under a hidden treatment in the static setting. Their framework uses a surrogate variable, together with an additional proxy variable related to the hidden treatment, and develops multiply robust estimators using semiparametric efficiency theory. Our work also leverages a proxy for the hidden action to identify the value function and construct an estimator. A key feature of the RL setting is that the next state provides such a proxy naturally: because it depends on the current latent action through the transition dynamics, it contains information about the hidden action that can be exploited for identification. Despite this connection, our setting differs substantially from that of Zhou and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2024) . First, hidden actions arise in a sequential decision-making setting. Consequently, the target parameter and nuisance functions depend on the transition dynamics and the target policy, making the problem substantially more complex than in the static setting. Second, unlike the static hidden-treatment setting, which requires an additional proxy variable, the next state in RL serves simultaneously as a proxy for the current hidden action and as part of the future trajectory. This dual role creates technical challenges that are absent in the single-stage setting. As a result, the identification strategy, influence-function derivation, and asymptotic analysis require new arguments that explicitly exploit the sequential nature of RL, rather than constituting a direct extension of the single-stage hidden-treatment framework. Challenges and contributions . Since the true action in the environment is never observed, off-policy evaluation with hidden actions presents three main challenges. First, the state–action distribution underlying standard OPE methods is latent, making it unclear whether the target policy value is identifiable from the observed data. Second, even when identification can be established, constructing valid estimators remains nontrivial, as naively substituting the latent action with its surrogate in existing OPE methods generally leads to biased estimates. Finally, valid uncertainty quantification and policy comparison procedures have yet to be developed in this setting. To address these challenges, we first establish identification of the target policy value in the presence of hidden actions by leveraging the next-state variable within the RL framework. Second, we derive an observed-data influence function representation and use it to construct LURE ( L earning from the U nseen: R obust E stimator), a multiply robust estimator that remains consistent under several combinations of correctly specified nuisance components. To address the unobserved latent-action problem in the estimation procedure, we propose a novel expectation–maximization-based algorithm for estimating the nuisance functions in our offline RL setting. Finally, we establish finite-sample error bounds and the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator, enabling valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for policy value estimation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to study offline reinforcement learning in the hidden-action setting. Organization . The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we review the standard RL framework and existing OPE methods. In Sections 3 and 4 , we introduce the hidden-action setting, establish identification, and construct the LURE estimator. In Section 5 , we present the large-sample theory for LURE. In Section 6 , we report simulation results, and in Section 7 we present the MIMIC-III sepsis analysis. We conclude with a discussion in Section 8 . All proofs are deferred to the Appendix. 2 Preliminaries In this section, we briefly review the standard RL framework, in which actions are perfectly recorded. The aforementioned OPE identification results and estimation methods all rely on the assumption that actions are perfectly measured in the offline data. In many applications, however, the decision-maker only has access to an error-prone observed action A ~ t ∈ 𝒜 \widetilde{A}_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , which is a noisy measurement of the underlying true action A t A_{t} . Naively substituting A ~ t \widetilde{A}_{t} for A t A_{t} in any of the above OPE methods will generally produce biased estimates, since the Q Q -function and density ratio are both defined with respect to the latent true action. We address this setting in the following section. 3 RL with Unobserved Action In our framework, the true actions A i , t A_{i,t} are not directly recorded. Instead, we observe trajectories of the form { ( S i , t , A ~ i , t , R i , t ) : 1 ≤ i ≤ N , 1 ≤ t ≤ T } \{(S_{i,t},\widetilde{A}_{i,t},R_{i,t}):1\leq i\leq N,\ 1\leq t\leq T\} , where A ~ i , t \widetilde{A}_{i,t} is an error-prone surrogate for the hidden action A i , t A_{i,t} . The core challenge is that the true action A A is unobserved, so standard estimating methods in existing RL cannot be applied directly. We address this via a novel EM-style ( Dempster et al., 1977 ) iterative procedure that alternates between (i) estimating nuisance functions given the current posterior probability (the “M-step”), and (ii) updating the posterior probability given the current nuisance estimates (the “E-step”).
